metadata.title: Guatemalan Spanish Lexicon for Codex
metadata.description: A Codex-friendly lexicon of Guatemalan Spanish words, phrases, food terms, voseo patterns, and coffee/café expressions. It prioritizes Guatemala-specific and strongly Guatemalan usage, while marking terms that are shared regionally or widespread but important in Guatemala.
metadata.important_note: No living dialect has a fixed complete list of all unique terms. This is a curated working lexicon, not an exhaustive dictionary. Use guatemala_specificity_score_1_to_5 and confidence fields when generating learner content.

specificity_scale.5: near-unique to Guatemala or a very strong Guatemalan cultural marker
specificity_scale.4: strongly associated with Guatemala, sometimes shared nearby
specificity_scale.3: shared Central American or broader Latin American term that is important in Guatemala
specificity_scale.2: widespread Spanish/Latin American term included because it appears in common Guatemalan interactions
specificity_scale.1: standard Spanish support phrase included for practical context

entries.example_es: Mi amiga es chapina y habla con mucho sabor local.
entries.example_en: My friend is Guatemalan and speaks with a lot of local flavor.
entries.notes: ASALE marks chapín/chapina as relating to Guatemala and Guatemalan speech.

entries.meaning_en: Guatemalanism; a Guatemalan word, phrase, habit, or linguistic feature
entries.meaning_es_neutral: guatemaltequismo; palabra o expresión propia del español de Guatemala
entries.example_en: 'Muchá' is a very useful Guatemalanism.
entries.notes: Use for project labels or tags.

entries.meaning_en: a Guatemalan-style act, custom, or joke
entries.meaning_es_neutral: costumbre, acción o broma de sabor guatemalteco
entries.example_es: Llevar tamales al convivio fue una chapinada bonita.
entries.example_en: Bringing tamales to the gathering was a nice Guatemalan touch.
entries.notes: Useful as a cultural tag; meanings vary by speaker.

entries.meaning_en: to Guatemalanize; to adapt something to Guatemalan usage
entries.meaning_es_neutral: adaptar algo al estilo o habla de Guatemala
entries.example_es: Voy a chapinizar estas frases para que suenen naturales.
entries.example_en: I’m going to Guatemalanize these phrases so they sound natural.
entries.notes: Good for Codex transformations of neutral Spanish into Guatemalan Spanish.

entries.example_en: You’re right.
entries.notes: Not unique to Guatemala, but central to natural Guatemalan Spanish.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: tú eres / usted es, en voseo informal
entries.example_en: You’re very sharp.
entries.notes: Use with trusted peers, family, and friends.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: tú tienes / usted tiene, en voseo informal
entries.example_es: Vos tenés pisto para el café?
entries.example_en: Do you have money for coffee?

entries.meaning_es_neutral: tú puedes / usted puede, en voseo informal
entries.example_en: Can you pick me up?
Do you want a coffee?

entries.example_es: Vení, muchá, ya sirvieron la refacción.
entries.example_en: Come on, guys, they’ve served the snack.

entries.example_es: Mirá, ese lugar tiene buen café de Antigua.
entries.example_en: Look, that place has good Antigua coffee.

entries.example_es: Hacé la cola mientras busco mesa.
entries.example_en: Get in line while I find a table.

entries.example_es: Andá a pedir dos aguas puras.
entries.example_en: Go order two bottles of water.
Sit down, the food is coming.
entries.notes: Voseo imperative without accent in common spelling; formally 'sentate' in voseo.

entries.example_en: Don’t leave, I’ll be right back.
The kid asked for a champurrada.
entries.notes: ASALE lists Guatemala and neighboring areas for the 'child' sense.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: grupo de niños; conducta de patojo
entries.example_es: La patojada salió a jugar chamusca.
entries.example_en: The kids went out to play pickup soccer.
entries.notes: Derived from patojo; common in casual speech.

entries.example_en: That kid is very sharp.
entries.notes: Often spelled ishto or ixto in informal writing.

entries.example_es: Cuando era güiro vivía en Xela.
entries.example_en: When I was a kid I lived in Xela.
entries.notes: Shared in parts of Central America.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: muchachos; grupo de amigos o personas
entries.example_en: Hey guys, what’s up?
entries.notes: One of the most useful Guatemalan address words for a group.

entries.example_en: Hey bro, shall we go get coffee?
entries.notes: Short for hermano; widespread but very common locally.

entries.example_es: Voy con mis aleros al mercado.
entries.example_en: I’m going with my buddies to the market.
entries.notes: Common in Central America; source lists 'aleros' with muchá.

entries.example_es: Mi cuate trabaja en una cafetería.
entries.example_en: My friend works in a coffee shop.
entries.notes: More broadly Mexican/Central American, still useful in Guatemala.

entries.meaning_en: group of people; crowd; gang depending on context
entries.meaning_es_neutral: grupo de gente; pandilla según contexto
entries.example_es: La mara llegó temprano al convivio.
entries.example_en: The group arrived early to the gathering.
entries.notes: Context decides whether it means people/friends or gang.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: miembro de una mara o pandilla
entries.example_es: El periodista evitó usar la palabra sin contexto.
entries.example_en: The journalist avoided using the word without context.
entries.notes: High-sensitivity term; avoid as a casual insult.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: persona rubia o de pelo claro
entries.example_es: El canche pidió café sin azúcar.
entries.example_en: The blond guy ordered coffee without sugar.
entries.notes: Common descriptor; can be neutral or teasing by tone.

entries.meaning_en: light-skinned or blond person; also beer in some contexts
entries.meaning_es_neutral: persona de piel clara o rubia; también cerveza según contexto
entries.example_es: La chela de la mesa pidió atol de elote.
entries.example_en: The fair-haired woman at the table ordered corn atol.
entries.notes: Meaning varies; in some countries chela = beer.

entries.example_es: Voy a cantinear a la chava.
entries.example_en: I’m going to flirt with the girl.
entries.notes: Widespread, but many Guatemalan phrases use it.

entries.example_es: Mi traída quiere ir por shucos.
entries.example_en: My girlfriend wants to go for Guatemalan hot dogs.
entries.notes: Informal and a bit old-school; also heard elsewhere.

entries.example_es: Dicen que anda con su cashpian.
entries.example_en: They say he’s with his lover.
entries.notes: Informal spelling varies; included with lower confidence.

entries.meaning_en: lover; sweetheart; regular customer/vendor relation depending on context
entries.meaning_es_neutral: querido o amante; también cliente habitual según contexto
entries.example_es: No le digás casera si no hay confianza.
entries.example_en: Don’t call her casera if there’s no trust.
entries.notes: RAE/Guatemala lists a lover sense; ordinary Spanish also uses customer/vendor senses.

entries.example_es: En la historia mencionaron a un cuque.
entries.example_en: In the story they mentioned a soldier.
entries.notes: May sound dismissive depending on tone.

entries.example_es: Viene el chonte, bajá la voz.
entries.example_en: The cop is coming, lower your voice.
The police are coming.
entries.notes: Widespread slang, included because common in Guatemalan phrase lists.

entries.example_en: Don’t be nosy, man.
entries.notes: ASALE lists the nosy-person sense for Guatemala.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: meterse o curiosear donde no corresponde
entries.example_en: Stop snooping through my phone.
entries.notes: Derived from shute; ASALE wheel lists shutear.

entries.example_en: That comment was really nosy.

entries.example_es: ¡Qué chilera está la vista del lago!
entries.example_en: The lake view is so cool/beautiful!
entries.notes: ASALE lists a Guatemala sense for things that are very good, excellent, or beautiful.

entries.example_es: La patoja es chispuda para vender.
entries.example_en: The girl is clever at selling.
entries.notes: ASALE lists Guatemala and nearby usage.

entries.meaning_en: alert, clever, capable; also 'hurry up' in phrases
entries.example_es: Ponete pilas que ya casi cierran.
entries.example_en: Get moving; they’re about to close.
entries.notes: Not unique, but essential in Guatemalan phrase use.

entries.meaning_en: smart; also head in some uses
entries.example_en: You’re really smart, huh.
That bag is sturdy.
entries.notes: Less universal than chilero; good for regional flavor.

entries.meaning_en: tough-skinned; shameless or able to take criticism
entries.meaning_es_neutral: que aguanta críticas; desvergonzado según contexto
entries.example_en: He has thick skin for criticism.
entries.notes: Guatemala.com lists cuerudo as a RAE-recognized chapinismo.

entries.example_en: —Is this the bus? —Exactly.
entries.notes: Some dictionaries list neighboring countries; Guatemalans use it heavily.

entries.example_en: The plan is great.
entries.notes: Widespread Spanish meaning is 'clear'; local slang is 'excellent'.

entries.example_en: That place is really cool!
entries.notes: Especially common in El Salvador too; include as regional-shared.

entries.example_en: The trip was great!
The handicraft is so pretty.
entries.notes: Widespread; included because source lists it in Guatemalan slang.

entries.example_en: Be quiet, they’re talking.
entries.caution: Rude if used with strangers or elders.
entries.notes: Can be rude depending on tone.

entries.meaning_en: wow, dang, gosh; surprise or frustration
entries.meaning_es_neutral: expresión de sorpresa, molestia o admiración
entries.example_en: Dang, that’s expensive!
Gosh, it’s already late!
Wow, man, what traffic!
entries.notes: Often in 'ala gran' or before a request.

entries.example_es: ¡A la gran, se me olvidó la billetera!
entries.example_en: Oh my, I forgot my wallet!

entries.meaning_es_neutral: expresión fuerte de sorpresa o asombro
entries.example_en: Good grief, what a line!
entries.notes: Colorful but not usually as vulgar as stronger alternatives.

entries.example_en: Yuck, that’s dirty!
entries.notes: Guatemala.com lists 'chis' as a RAE-recognized chapinismo.

entries.example_en: There’s drizzle in Cobán.
entries.notes: Guatemala.com lists it among RAE-recognized chapinismos.

entries.meaning_en: strong afternoon wind, especially around Lake Atitlán
entries.meaning_es_neutral: viento fuerte de la tarde, especialmente del lago de Atitlán
entries.example_es: El xocomil empezó después de almuerzo.
entries.example_en: The afternoon wind started after lunch.

entries.meaning_en: to press or push, especially a button
entries.example_en: Press the doorbell button.
entries.notes: Guatemala.com lists apachar as a RAE-recognized chapinismo.

entries.example_es: Ese plan está un poco achusemado.
entries.example_en: That plan is a bit crazy.
Don’t water down the coffee.
They stole my umbrella.

entries.meaning_en: overly devout Catholic; sometimes very conservative
entries.meaning_es_neutral: católico que aparenta mucha devoción; muy conservador según contexto
entries.example_es: Mi abuela dice que ese señor es cachureco.
entries.example_en: My grandmother says that man is very devout/conservative.
entries.notes: Guatemala.com gives a religious-devotion sense; political sense may vary.

entries.meaning_en: skipping class; absent from school to wander
entries.example_es: Se fue capeado con sus amigos.
entries.example_en: He skipped class with his friends.

entries.example_es: Se hizo un chongo para el calor.
entries.example_en: She put her hair in a bun because of the heat.

entries.meaning_en: to look at; to discredit or expose depending on context
entries.example_es: No me choteés enfrente de todos.
entries.example_en: Don’t expose/embarrass me in front of everyone.
entries.notes: Definitions vary; Guatemala.com notes both looking and discrediting senses.

entries.example_en: We used to play marbles in the street.

entries.example_es: Compró un cuto en la tienda.
entries.example_en: He bought a small bottle of liquor at the store.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: sucio; cerdo o carne de cerdo según contexto
entries.example_es: No pongás eso ahí, está coche.
entries.example_en: Don’t put that there, it’s dirty.
entries.notes: Guatemala.com lists 'coche' as dirty; local lists also use carne de coche for pork.

entries.meaning_en: to involve someone in something harmful or compromising
entries.meaning_es_neutral: involucrar a alguien en algo que lo perjudica
entries.example_es: No me embroqués en ese clavo.
entries.example_en: Don’t drag me into that problem.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: conversación o discurso extenso e insustancial
entries.example_en: Lots of talk and little action.

entries.meaning_en: drunk; also blood sausage in food contexts
entries.meaning_es_neutral: borracho; también embutido de sangre según contexto
entries.example_en: He left the party drunk.
entries.notes: Guatemala.com gives a drunk sense; food sense exists too.

entries.meaning_en: drunkenness / getting drunk in some expressions
entries.meaning_es_neutral: borrachera o acción de emborracharse según contexto
entries.example_es: La matraca les duró todo el fin de semana.
entries.example_en: Their drinking spree lasted all weekend.
entries.notes: Often appears with moronga in source lists.

entries.example_es: No seas clavero con ese tema.
entries.example_en: Don’t be reckless/troublesome with that topic.

entries.example_es: No fui jute; revisé el recibo.
entries.example_en: I wasn’t naive; I checked the receipt.
Don’t be stingy, leave a tip.
That phone is ugly/bad quality.
entries.caution: Insulting if aimed at a person.
entries.notes: Can be insulting when used for people.

entries.example_en: That comment was tacky.
entries.notes: Can carry classist tone; use carefully.

entries.example_es: No seas caquero con el carro.
entries.example_en: Don’t show off with the car.
entries.notes: Common slang label for pretentious behavior.

entries.example_en: That place is kind of posh.
entries.notes: Low confidence; included from one source list.

entries.meaning_en: low quality, fake, bad; also military in some lists
entries.meaning_es_neutral: de mala calidad; del ejército según contexto
entries.example_en: That charger is cheap/low quality.
entries.notes: Widespread; Guatemalan lists include military sense too.

entries.example_es: Qué gacho que te quedaran mal.
entries.example_en: That’s rough that they let you down.
The exam was really hard.
The internet is slow.
Don’t trust that shady guy.
Don’t be dumb, read carefully.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: torpe, que hace mal las cosas
entries.example_en: I’m clumsy at dancing.
entries.notes: Source glosses as lelo; broader Spanish also uses it.

entries.example_en: Don’t act like a fool.
entries.notes: Not unique, but appears in local lists.

entries.example_es: No seas mula; mirá antes de cruzar.
entries.example_en: Don’t be stupid; look before crossing.
entries.caution: Insulting unless playful among close friends.

entries.meaning_en: jerk, worthless person; also familiar rough address among close friends
entries.meaning_es_neutral: insulto fuerte; trato brusco entre amigos según confianza
entries.example_en: That jerk didn’t pay.
entries.notes: Highly context-dependent; may be friendly among close friends but offensive otherwise.

entries.meaning_en: screwed, in trouble; exploited or betrayed person
entries.meaning_es_neutral: jodido, en problema; persona traicionada según contexto
entries.example_es: Estoy pisado si no entrego eso hoy.
entries.example_en: I’m screwed if I don’t turn that in today.
Don’t be lazy, help.
He was gutsy to speak clearly.

entries.example_es: Ese café está de a huevo.
entries.example_en: That coffee is great.
entries.notes: Extremely common but vulgar; not for formal settings.

entries.meaning_en: by force, whether you want to or not
entries.example_en: They did it by force.

entries.meaning_en: joking around; mischief; fun; annoying thing depending on context
entries.meaning_es_neutral: broma, diversión, molestia o cosa según contexto
entries.example_en: Enough messing around; let’s work.

entries.meaning_en: hit, blow; also a lot of something in some contexts
entries.example_es: Me di un pijazo en la rodilla.
entries.example_en: I hit my knee hard.
Don’t provoke him; he’s angry.

entries.meaning_en: to beat up; to fight hard
entries.example_en: They say they beat him up.
entries.notes: Violent slang; use only when appropriate.

entries.example_en: In that story they said, 'they’ll kill you.'
That guy is a lowlife.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: perro; tacaño o aprovechado según contexto
entries.example_es: Ese chucho siempre quiere más descuento.
entries.example_en: That greedy guy always wants more discount.
entries.notes: Dog sense is ordinary; stingy/greedy sense is locally important.

entries.meaning_en: cat; shy/timid person in some contexts
entries.example_es: El mish se escondió debajo de la mesa.
entries.example_en: The cat hid under the table.
entries.notes: Spelling and senses vary; included from local lists.

entries.example_es: El kak'ik se prepara con chompipe.
entries.example_en: Kak'ik is prepared with turkey.
entries.notes: ASALE lists chompipe/chumpipe for Guatemala and neighboring countries.

entries.meaning_en: scapegoat; the one blamed for everything
entries.example_es: Siempre lo hacen chompipe de la fiesta.
entries.example_en: They always make him the scapegoat.
entries.notes: ASALE lists this phrase for Guatemala and nearby countries.

entries.example_es: No tengo pisto para el taxi.
entries.example_en: I don’t have money for the taxi.
Did you bring money?
entries.notes: Widespread Latin America; common in Guatemala.

entries.meaning_en: one quetzal; money in general by context
entries.example_es: Dame una vara para el bus.
entries.example_en: Give me one quetzal for the bus.
entries.notes: Spelling often 'vara'; source has 'bara' in informal spelling.

entries.example_es: Traigo lenes para pagar la camioneta.
entries.example_en: I brought coins to pay for the bus.
entries.notes: Listed in local sources as moneda.

entries.example_en: I need a coin to make up the amount.

entries.meaning_en: small coin; often 25 centavos by local usage
entries.example_en: I’m short one small coin.
entries.notes: Local value references may vary by generation/context.

entries.example_es: Dame un tostón y te doy vuelto.
entries.example_en: Give me a fifty and I’ll give you change.
entries.notes: Money slang varies by country; source glosses Q50.

entries.example_en: That repair cost a ton of money.

entries.example_es: No tengo plante para salir hoy.
entries.example_en: I don’t have money to go out today.
entries.notes: Often in phrase 'no tengo plante o varas'.

entries.example_en: Let’s pool money for the pizza.
entries.notes: Common in Guatemala and nearby countries.

entries.example_es: Tomé la camioneta para ir al centro.
entries.example_en: I took the bus to go downtown.
entries.notes: In Guatemala, camioneta commonly means bus, not just van/pickup.

entries.example_es: Me fui en burra hasta la zona 1.
entries.example_en: I took the bus to Zone 1.

entries.example_es: El turista tomó un chicken bus a Antigua.
entries.example_en: The tourist took a chicken bus to Antigua.
entries.notes: English-origin term used by travelers and sometimes locals.

entries.example_en: Watch out for the speed bump.
Where is the parking lot?
Can you give me a ride to the market?

entries.meaning_es_neutral: llevar a alguien en carro; dar aventón
entries.example_es: Mi primo me dio jalón hasta la capital.
entries.example_en: My cousin gave me a ride to the capital.

entries.example_es: Demos un colazo por el lago.
entries.example_en: Let’s take a ride around the lake.
entries.notes: Not unique, but useful for local plans.

entries.example_en: I’m going to the capital tomorrow.
I’m going home.
I’m going to work early.
Shall we watch a movie?
Bring a jacket because there’s drizzle.
Bring your jacket.

entries.example_es: Mis rieles están llenos de lodo.
entries.example_en: My shoes are full of mud.

entries.example_es: Me manché el caballo con café.
entries.example_en: I stained my pants with coffee.
entries.notes: Listed in local phrase sources; use with lower confidence.

entries.example_es: Cuidá tus chivas en el bus.
entries.example_en: Watch your things on the bus.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: cosa cuyo nombre no se recuerda
entries.example_es: Pasame ese cuenteraile de la mesa.
entries.example_en: Pass me that thingamajig from the table.
They brought a pitcher of juice/soda drink.
Could I have a straw?
entries.notes: Not in the retrieved lists but common Central American usage; included with medium confidence.

entries.example_en: That’s a lie.
entries.notes: Common in Guatemala; can be blunt.

entries.example_en: Don’t believe him; he’s a liar.
Don’t feed me lies.
That deal smells shady.

entries.example_es: Tengo un clavo con la tarjeta.
entries.example_en: I have a problem with the card.
That paperwork is really complicated.

entries.example_es: Llegamos a las ocho, sin clavos.
entries.example_en: We’ll arrive at eight, no problem.
entries.notes: Natural extension of clavo; common colloquial phrase.

entries.meaning_en: to get lucky; to do well
entries.example_en: He got lucky with that price.
What luck that you found parking!
entries.notes: Source spelling 'wasa'; normalized here as guasa/wasa.

entries.example_en: I’m scared to get up there.

entries.example_es: Me dio basca en la camioneta.
entries.example_en: I got nauseous on the bus.
I have a hangover from the party.
entries.notes: Core Central American word for hangover.

entries.example_es: Mi tío salió bolo del convivio.
entries.example_en: My uncle left the gathering drunk.
He got really drunk.
I’m going to throw up.
entries.notes: Appears in phrase 'ir a amarrar buitre'.

entries.example_en: The trip made him vomit.
We played pickup soccer in the afternoon.
entries.notes: Very common social/sports term; not in retrieved snippets but strongly associated.

entries.example_en: A party got going.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: comida o reunión por algún acontecimiento
entries.example_es: Tenemos convivio de fin de año.
entries.example_en: We have an end-of-year gathering.

entries.meaning_en: snack, light refreshment; school/work break snack
entries.example_es: A media mañana nos dieron refacción.
entries.example_en: Mid-morning they gave us a snack.
What’s up, man?
What’s up, man, shall we go for coffee?
entries.notes: Combines wider 'qué onda' with local voseo.

entries.example_en: What’s up, man, all good?
entries.notes: Spelling also 'quiúbole' elsewhere; this compact form is casual.

entries.example_en: That market is so cool!
entries.notes: High-value phrase for natural positive reactions.

entries.example_en: Your project is so cool!

entries.meaning_en: come on; hurry up; be sharp
entries.example_es: ¡Pilas pues, que ya sale la camioneta!
entries.example_en: Come on, the bus is leaving!

entries.meaning_en: get moving; pay attention; be sharp
entries.example_en: Pay attention to the receipt.

entries.meaning_en: do me a favor; help me out
entries.example_es: Haceme el paro y guardame lugar.
entries.example_en: Do me a favor and save me a spot.

entries.meaning_en: do me a favor; help me out
entries.example_en: Hey, do me a favor.

entries.meaning_en: please give me a soda/soft drink
entries.example_en: Please give me an orange soda/drink.
entries.notes: In Guatemala 'me regala/regáleme' is a common polite transaction formula.

entries.example_es: Regáleme un agua pura sin gas.
entries.example_en: Please give me still bottled water.
entries.notes: Very useful in cafes and tiendas.

entries.meaning_es_neutral: ¿me da...?, fórmula cortés de compra o solicitud
entries.example_en: Could you give me a bag, please?

entries.meaning_en: well, the thing is...; often introduces an excuse or explanation
